en: The Seven Buddhas’ Verses from the Mind-Lamp of the Buddhas and Patriarchs: Vipaśyin Buddha (the 998th of the past *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa*)
The body arises from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion;
The illusory person’s mind and consciousness are fundamentally non-existent, And both sin and merit are empty, with nothing to abide in.
Śikhin Buddha (the nine hundred and ninety-ninth honored one of the *Vyūha-kalpa*).
The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; The commission of all unwholesome karmas is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind. Illusory appearances have no root and possess no real nature.
Vipaśyin Buddha (the first of the thousand Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa*).
Borrowing the four great elements to form a body, the mind is fundamentally unborn, arising only due to external objects;
if the objects before one do not exist, the mind likewise does not exist. Transgressions and blessings are like illusions, arising and then ceasing.
Kāśyapa Buddha (the first honored one of the present Bhadrakalpa).
To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion.
When one realizes that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty, How does such a person differ from the Buddha?
Kanakamuni Buddha (the second honored one of the Bhadrakalpa).
The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; If there were such a knowing, there would be no Buddha apart from it.
The wise one can know that the nature of sin is empty; He remains serene and is not terrified by birth and death.
Kāśyapa Buddha (the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa).
The minds of all sentient beings are pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa).
The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma; Without Dharma, even Dharma is Dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting the absence of Dharma, In all dharmas, when has there ever been "Dharma"?
This is the verse on transmitting the Dharma by the thirty-third patriarch.
Mahākāśyapa (the First Patriarch of India):
The Dharma is the original nature of all dharmas; There is no dharma, nor is there any non-dharma. How could there be both dharma and non-dharma within a single dharma?
Ānanda (the second patriarch of India) originally possessed the Dharma;
having transmitted it, he said there was no Dharma. Each must awaken for themselves;
once awakened, there is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma.
Śāṇakavāsa (the Third Patriarch of India):
Neither dharma nor mind, Neither mind nor dharma. When these "mind-dharmas" are spoken of, These dharmas are not mind-dharmas.
Upagupta (the Fourth Patriarch of India):

The mind is from the very beginning the original mind; The original mind is not a dharma that exists. If there were a dharma that existed, there would be an original mind; But since it is not a mind, it is not an original dharma.
Dhitika (the Fifth Patriarch of India) thoroughly realized the Dharma of the original mind: There is neither dharma nor non-dharma; Awakening is the same as non-awakening;
Without mind and without dharma.
Mīzhajiā (the sixth patriarch of India):

When there is no mind, there is nothing to be attained; What is spoken cannot be called a dharma. If one realizes that the mind is not the mind, Only then does one truly understand the mind and its dharmas.
Vasumitra (the Seventh Patriarch of India):
His mind is identical to the realm of empty space; he demonstrates dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, there is neither "is" nor "non-is."
Buddha Nandi (the Eighth Patriarch of India):
Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one realizes the nature of space, One thereby penetrates the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Vajramitra (the Ninth Patriarch of India):
True reality is not nameless; through names, true reality is revealed. Having received the true Dharma, it is neither true nor false.
The Venerable Pārśva (the Tenth Patriarch of India):
The true body is naturally real; Because it is real, there is a principle to be explained. Having realized the truly real Dharma, there is neither practice nor cessation.
Punyananda (the Eleventh Patriarch): Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation;
light and darkness are not separate from one another. Now I transmit this Dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two.
The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa (the Twelfth Patriarch):
manifestation and concealment are precisely this Dharma; light and darkness are fundamentally non-dual. Now, I entrust this realization:
the Dharma is neither grasped nor abandoned.
Kāpimāla (the thirteenth patriarch) taught that the dharma is neither hidden nor manifest;
he declared this to be the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). One who awakens to this dharma of non-hiddenness and non-manifestness is neither foolish nor wise.
The Venerable Nāgārjuna (the Fourteenth Patriarch),
in order to clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, spoke thus of the logic of liberation: regarding all phenomena, the mind does not realize them as objects,
being neither angry nor joyful.

Kāṇadeva (the Fifteenth Patriarch), originally facing those who would receive the Dharma transmission, expounded for them the principle of liberation: regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing realized;
it has no end and no beginning.
Rāhulabhadra (the sixteenth patriarch):

Regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; it is neither grasped nor abandoned. Since the Dharma has no characteristics of existence or non-existence, how could it arise internally or externally?
Saṃghanandin (the Seventeenth Patriarch):
The ground of the mind is fundamentally without arising; The causal ground arises from conditions. Condition and seed do not obstruct one another;
Flowers and fruits are likewise so.
Gayāsata (the eighteenth patriarch) has a seed and a ground of mind;
through causes and conditions, it is able to sprout. When there is no mutual obstruction among conditions, that which is about to arise is non-arising.
Kumāralāta (the nineteenth patriarch):

In the ultimate nature, there is fundamentally no birth; it is only for the sake of those seeking [enlightenment] that I speak. Since there is nothing to be attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts about what is resolved or unresolved?
Śāṇakavāsa (the Twentieth Patriarch) said:

"In the moment of hearing [the teaching], one accords with the non-arising; it is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand in this way, one will penetrate the realms of both phenomena and principle."
Vasu-bandhu (the twenty-first patriarch):
When foam and illusions are equally unimpeded, how can one fail to awaken? To penetrate the Dharma within this is neither of the present nor of the past.
Maṇḍara (the twenty-second patriarch):
The mind turns following the myriad objects; Where it turns is truly profound. Recognizing one's nature as it flows with the current, There is neither joy nor sorrow.
When Hellenā (the twenty-third patriarch) recognized the nature of mind,
it could be called inconceivable; when it is clearly understood that there is nothing to be attained,
one does not speak of knowing.
When the Bhikṣu Siṃha (the twenty-fourth patriarch) correctly expounded that knowledge and vision are both the mind, then within the mind there is knowledge and vision,
and knowledge and vision are right here and now.
The Holy One Vasiṣṭha (the twenty-fifth patriarch) spoke of knowing and seeing:
when confronted with objects, there is neither right nor wrong; I have now awakened to the true nature, wherein there is neither the Way nor principle.
Ratnamati (the twenty-sixth patriarch):
The true nature is the treasury of the mind-ground; It has neither head nor tail. Responding to conditions to transform sentient beings, it is expediently called "wisdom."
Prajñātāra (the twenty-seventh patriarch):
The mind-ground gives birth to all seeds; Due to conditions, they arise again. When the fruit is full, bodhi is perfected;
When the flower opens, the world emerges.
Bodhidharma (the twenty-eighth patriarch in the Western Heaven and the first patriarch in China):
I have come to this land to transmit the Dharma and save those lost in delusion; When the one flower blooms into five petals, the fruit will naturally be formed.
The Great Master Huike (the Twenty-ninth Patriarch, the Second Patriarch of China):
Originally there was ground for conditions; Based on that ground, flowers were planted and grew. Originally there was no ground;
Flowers were never planted, nor were they ever born.
Master Sengcan (The Thirtieth Patriarch, the Third Patriarch of China):
Though the flower-seed depends on the earth, From the earth the flower grows. If there were no one to sow the seed, The earth would be entirely without flowers.
Master Daoxin (the thirty-first patriarch, the fourth patriarch of China):
The nature of the lotus seed has the capacity for birth; Because of the ground, the lotus is born again and again. When the great condition unites with faith, Birth after birth becomes non-birth.
Master Hongren (the Thirty-second Patriarch, the Fifth Patriarch of China):
"When sentient beings come to plant seeds, The fruit arises according to the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, They lack nature and thus have no arising."
Master Huineng (the Thirty-third Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch of China):
The mind-ground contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the delusions of the flowers are suddenly awakened to, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously realized.
The Genealogy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs: Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Śāṇavāsa, Upagupta,
and Dhitika, Kātyāyanīputra, Vasumitra, Pārśva, Aśvaghoṣa, and Mātṛceṭa.
Nāgārjuna and Kāṇadeva at Rāhu; Saṃghagaya, Kumārajīva, Yaśa, Vasumitra, and Śrīmat;
Siṃha and Vāsabandhu transmitted [the teachings] to the Eastern Lands; thereafter came Huiyuan, Sengdao, and Daohong.
